description: Our goal is to visualize NASA data so that anyone, anywhere can understand and make good use of it.
summary:
We developed Earth Systems Detective, an interactive 3D globe that turns NASA Earth observation data into plain-English answers. The user spins the Earth, chooses a region, and the terrain separates into three layers: atmosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere/biosphere. They then select one variable from any layer and any other variable, such as precipitation and soil moisture, to investigate how Earth’s systems affect each other.

A graph plots both variables over time, while data analysis runs to calculate the rate of change of the variables and tests significance to separate trends from random change. The results are translated into a clear verdict, with simple definitions and real-world impacts. The tool also auto-detects the user’s location and shows whether a chosen crop or industry suits it, suggesting better nearby locations when it doesn’t.

This matters because NASA’s data is powerful but hard for most people to interpret. By making it visual, interactive, and understandable to anyone, including students, farmers, and communities, our tool helps people make better decisions about their land and its future.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Data made easy! starts with a 3D Earth. You spin it, click a region, and the ground separates into three layers: air, water, and land. Click the air layer and you can pick a variable such precipitation. Click the land layer and you can pick another variable such as soil moisture. You can then compare both side by side on a graph or read the verdict shown next to it.

We also added a last step where the app finds your location, asks if you want to plant something or start an industry and then it tells you whether the place suits it or not. If it doesn’t, it points to somewhere nearby that does.

What benefits does it have?

NASA data is free, but most people can’t use it. They’d have to know the acronyms for variables, download files, and run the data analysis themselves. Our tool does that for them so that a student or a farmer or anyone in general can see what’s happening to a specific area of land and what it means.

What is the intended impact?

We want more people to use NASA’s Earth data, and to see that rain, soil, and air are connected. We also want it to help with real decisions. A farmer choosing a crop shouldn’t have to guess whether the rainfall is trending the wrong way.

What tools did we use?

Data: We use NASA Earth observation data accessed through NASA’s open APIs. NASA’s Common Metadata Repository (CMR) lets us search and locate datasets. GPM provides precipitation, SMAP provides soil moisture, and MODIS provides vegetation, land surface temperature and aerosol data. NASA POWER supplies temperature, rainfall and humidity time series for any location, and NASA GIBS supplies satellite imagery layers for the globe.

How is it creative?

Most tools for NASA data are built for scientists. We built ours so that anyone can use it. There are no menus to learn and no acronyms to decode. You turn the globe and click where you live. Pulling the Earth apart into air, water, and land layers lets you see how the systems connect, even if you’ve never taken a science class. You pick variables by touching the layer they belong to, and the plain-English verdict turns the statistics into a sentence anyone can read. That last part matters most to us, because the data is only useful if people can understand it.

What factors did our team consider?

Mostly, whether someone with no science background could follow it. We tested that against a simple standard: could an elementary school student understand the verdict? We also didn’t want to overclaim. Two variables can’t tell you everything about whether land suits a crop, since soil type, elevation, and water access matter too, so the suitability result is advice and not a guarantee. We kept the first version focused on one clear investigation and added the location feature on top, and the same design can grow to more regions, variables, and crops.
